Science.title: Low testosterone linked to 18% higher risk of dying from cancer
Science.summary: A major international study tracking more than 26,000 men found that very low testosterone levels were associated with an 18% higher risk of dying from cancer later in life. Surprisingly, testosterone itself showed no clear link to prostate cancer, although two other sex hormones did. Researchers believe low testosterone could be an important early warning sign of future health risks, particularly when levels fall below 8.6 nmol/L.

Culture.title: Bluey’s Daley Pearson on how losing his brother inspired his new film: ‘He was the best thing ever to me’
Culture.summary: Allen, the first live-action film from Pearson’s Ludo Studio, follows a man who met an alien as a kid – and becomes obsessed with bringing him back Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email If, for whatever reason, you want to feel a bit sad, think too hard about what Elliott from ET would have been like as an adult. Or Coraline, or Matilda, or Chihiro, or those kids in Mary Poppins. The most amazing thing that ever happened in their lives – magic nanny, alien friend, psychic abilities, otherworldly adventures – was already over when they were kids. If that bad Harry Potter play taught us anything, they probably all grew into loser adults. This is the central premise for Allen, a new Netflix family film by Daley Pearson, co-founder of Ludo Studio, the Brisbane production company behind a little show called Bluey. As a kid growing up in the small coastal town of Coolum, Petey (TJ Power) happens across a friendly, bug-eyed extraterrestrial; the little guy can’t quite pronounce “alien”, so they settle on “Allen”. Petey and Allen are best pals for one blissful month, sharing a love for Cheezels, VHS and board games – until suddenly, Allen is summoned home. Decades later, Petey is trapped in a state of arrested development and obsession that frustrates everyone around him – until Allen returns, for surprising reasons I will not spoil here. Continue reading...

Culture.title: Iphigénie en Tauride review – stylised staging of opera of bloodthirsty priestesses and divine intervention
Culture.summary: Coliseum, London English National Opera’s production of Gluck’s opera has strong leads in Christine Rice, Nick Pritchard and Jacques Imbrailo. But why is it sung in French? Human sacrifice first; ask questions later. The story of Iphigénie among the Taurians, adapted from Euripides by Gluck and his librettist Guillard in 1779, is being told at English National Opera for the first time. It’s sung in French – more on that later – and staged by Lyndsey Turner, whose sparky Noyes Fludde won the company an Olivier award back in 2020. Within the narrow rectangular frame of Soutra Gilmour’s set, Iphigénie is one of many identical priestesses, all dressed in rippling folds of wine-red and lit in evening tones by Tim Mitchell (lighting that on opening night grew suddenly even dimmer in King Thoas’s aria, when a glitch brought things to a brief halt). Her job is to sacrifice to Diana any stranger who washes up on the shore, and her next victim may be her unrecognised brother Orestes. It takes divine intervention from Diana to make this all come good. At Coliseum, London, until 14 November Continue reading...
